title: SQL COUNT: Why Your Report Misses Rows
head: Four rows. Two counted.
The source values
Missing values
Count every row
Compare the totals
Choose the measure
spoken: Why did the report count only two rows?
Our small local table contains four records. Two have a number, and two have missing values. We want to count how many records arrived, not just how many contain a number.
Counting a column counts only values that are not missing. Here, the result is two. The other two records still exist in the table.
To count every record, use the star form shown on screen. It counts rows, including rows that contain missing values. We can also calculate how many values are missing by subtracting the two counts.
The actual result is four records, two recorded values and two missing values. We check those results against the original data.
Both forms are useful. Choose the total row count for records received, and the column count for values recorded. Neither should silently replace the other in a report.
notes: The star form counts all rows.
Four total; two recorded; two missing.
Choose the measure your report needs.

title: SQL UNION Can Remove Real Transactions
head: One row vanished
Two input lists
Duplicate removal
Keep every record
Compare row counts
Choose your intent
spoken: One row vanished when we combined the results.
Here are two small lists of values. The first has two entries and the second also has two. One value occurs in both. These represent invented records, not real transactions.
The union operation removes duplicate result rows. That can be exactly what you want for a unique list. But if each row represents a separate event, removing duplicates can change the total.
Use the all form to preserve every row returned by both queries. We execute the two expressions on the same input and compare the output.
The unique list contains three rows. The full list contains four rows, including both occurrences of the repeated value. The assertion confirms the difference.
Choose the operation that matches your data model. If records have distinct identifiers, include those identifiers when needed. Duplicate output values do not always mean duplicate events.
notes: Three unique rows; four total rows.
